problem: "Its bandwidth is set near the bit rate" is misleading. In receiver design the post-detection filter bandwidth is normally taken as roughly half the bit rate (Nyquist) up to about 0.7B; a filter as wide as B passes much more noise and costs sensitivity. A student may read this as 'filter bandwidth = B'.
fix: "Its bandwidth is set to roughly half the bit rate, at most about 0.7B, so noise is limited without smearing the pulses."

problem: The noise entry 'about 4kT/R_L' has no units and gives a mean-square spectral density, while the transimpedance text two paragraphs later gives the rms value √(4kT/R_f). The same quantity appears in two different forms, which confuses students comparing the rows.
fix: Give units in the table and use one form throughout, e.g. 'Noise current density √(4kT/R_L) A/√Hz (mean-square 4kT/R_L A²/Hz)'.

where: Section 3, derivation paragraph before the P ≈ Qσ/R formula
problem: 'The signal photocurrent is then about Qσ' is loose. The on-level photocurrent is 2Qσ if the off-level is taken as zero and the levels are 2Qσ apart; Qσ is the average (midpoint) photocurrent, which is what the formula P ≈ Qσ/R actually uses.
fix: "With the off-level at zero the on-level photocurrent is 2Qσ, so the average photocurrent is Qσ. The average received power is then P ≈ Qσ/R."

problem: The range '−25 to −40 dBm at a few hundred Mbit/s' is optimistic at the low end; around −40 dBm is reached by low-capacitance high-impedance front ends at much lower bit rates, not at a few hundred Mbit/s.
fix: "Practical PIN receivers reach about −25 to −32 dBm at a few hundred Mbit/s, and nearer −40 dBm only at lower bit rates or with a very low-capacitance front end."

problem: 'The thermal noise current falls by √2' can be read as 'falls by an amount √2' instead of 'falls by a factor of √2'.
fix: "The rms thermal noise current falls by a factor of √2 (to 1/√2 of its value) because it scales as √(4kT/R_f), and the bandwidth halves."
